articles.title: From the dark fleet to Russian diesel, there are no ‘silver bullets’ for bringing down fuel prices
articles.summary: Fuel prices are historically high and voters are taking out their anger on President Donald Trump and Republicans.
articles.body: Fuel prices are historically high and voters are taking out their anger on President Donald Trump and Republicans. Trump is waging a campaign in the final moments of the midterm election to quell discontent among farmers, truckers and drivers exhausted by $4 gas and near-record diesel. In the past few weeks, Trump officials have unveiled a wide range of policy moves, including an $8 billion lifeline to farmers, a controversial plan to import diesel from Russia, allowing truckers to use red-dyed diesel and ways to rehab the aging armada of dark-fleet tankers. The last-minute scramble to contain the energy price fallout is an implicit acknowledgement of how the war with Iran has exacerbated the American public’s yearslong frustration with the high cost of living – a problem Trump promised to fix on Day One. “It looks and feels panicky because they’re panicked,” said Douglas Holtz-Eakin, president of the American Action Forum, a center-right think tank. “They can’t move the price of diesel in the next 14 days. They have to hope they can convince voters to give them another chance.” Some of the Trump administration’s actions could be helpful, but none of them will give voters what they crave: Cheap gas, diesel and jet fuel. “There are no silver bullets here. None of them will solve the underlying problem,” said Bob McNally, a former energy adviser to President George W. Bush. McNally, founder and president of Rapidan Energy Group, said Republicans and Democrats alike look under every rock for solutions. “Few things terrify a sitting president more than high and rising pump prices – especially in an election year,” he said. “I have to say, I give this administration credit. They are looking under more rocks than most.” A(nother) bailout for farmers The latest move came on Monday night on the campaign trail in Kansas where Trump announced an $8 billion lifeline for farmers. The US Department of Agriculture said the one-time payments for American farmers this harvest season will “provide relief during temporary market disruptions and increased input costs.” Diesel prices have skyrocketed from $3.76 a gallon nationally before the war to an all-time high of $6.53 a gallon in late September. The spike has been especially painful for farmers, who need diesel to power their tractors and other farm equipment and also rely on diesel-powered trucks to get their food to market. Consider that the typical farm in Kansas spent about $31,000 on diesel last year – a hefty cost that could double this year, according to Gregg Ibendahl, associate professor of agricultural economics at Kansas State University. “Farming has gotten a lot more expensive – and it was expensive to start with,” said Ibendahl. Beyond the diesel spike, farmers are grappling with surging costs for fertilizer, another critical input made pricier by the war with Iran. Details on the $8 billion farmer rescue are fuzzy – the USDA says it won’t announcement payment rates for farmers until next month – but experts say the aid appears to be meaningful. Gabriel Lade, a professor focusing on agricultural economics at The Ohio State University, said the $8 billion rescue will provide “a good amount of money” to farmers but cautioned that ad-hoc payments like this tend to be poorly targeted. “Some farmers may come out ahead, others will still be behind,” Lade said. The Trump administration’s fuel rescue for farmers comes less than a year after the federal government paid farmers $12 billion through the Farmer Bridge Assistance Program. Lade said these farmer rescues have become a feature of America’s farm economy. “We are stuck in a situation where trade wars are depressing output prices and now real wars are raising input prices,” Lade said. Diesel from Russia Trump’s plan to import diesel from Russia sparked a bipartisan backlash and skepticism from researchers who say it amounts to little more than a band-aid. The initial plan calls for importing about 2.2 million barrels of diesel, a drop in the bucket of the roughly 4 million barrels the United States consumes each day (including heating oil). “If we imported all those barrels in one day, it would only last us until about lunch,” said Robert Yawger, director of energy futures at Mizuho Securities. Diesel prices are a few pennies higher today than when Trump announced the plan, underscoring the skepticism that the war-hobbled Russian refinery system has the firepower to ramp up exports. Dyed diesel for truckers At a campaign event in Nebraska earlier this month, Trump signed an executive order allowing truckers to use cheaper red-dyed diesel normally reserved for farmers. Analysts said the move could be helpful for semi-truck drivers because it will temporarily shield them from the federal tax of 24.4 cents per gallon of diesel for highway use. However, they cautioned it won’t be a game-changer because states also tax diesel for highway use. Some states have paused their diesel taxes, while others have not. That creates complexity and risk for truckers crossing state lines. Dark fleet to the rescue? Trump officials are also pushing another out-of-the-box idea designed to address high fuel prices: Bringing the dark fleet of sanctioned tankers out of the shadows. Energy Secretary Chris Wright, speaking at an event in New York on Monday, said the Trump administration is working with investors to buy, clean up and deploy idled sanctioned tankers. “We’re going to move some of the ships from what I call the ‘bad-guy fleet’ to the ‘good-guy fleet,” Wright told Bloomberg News. The focus on the dark fleet is designed to address the skyrocketing cost of shipping. The daily rate to hire an oil supertanker to move crude from the Persian Gulf to China has exploded from about $65,000 last year to $1.4 million this week, according to Clarksons Research. But deploying dark fleet vessels is easier said than done. It will require navigating a legal maze, convincing insurers to get on board and, in many cases, expensive repairs to aging tankers. “This will likely only have a small impact because many of these vessels are already being used. The ones that aren’t are probably old and in bad condition,” McNally said. How to drive down fuel prices None of the energy policy moves on their own or collectively will make gas and diesel cheap again. The Iran war, along with the Russia-Ukraine war and Houthi attacks in the Red Sea, have created a supply chain nightmare that will take considerable time to fix. Global energy markets are likely more than a year away from returning to normal, the head of the International Energy Agency warned on Tuesday. “The only things that will cause an immediate decline in prices would be a recession – which is not the way anyone wants to do it – or a durable, credible peace deal,” McNally said. “And unfortunately, we don’t see that as likely.”

articles.title: How higher bond yields are threatening the AI-fueled stock rally
articles.summary: Bond yields in the U.S. have risen this year, slowing down a stock market that has risen for years on the back of the AI build-out. After consistently rising, with a few exceptions, from late March through mid-August, the S&P 500 is down nearly 90 points from Oct. 7. The Nasdaq composite, meanwhile, is down…
articles.body:
Bond yields in the U.S. have risen this year, slowing down a stock market that has risen for years on the back of the AI build-out .

After consistently rising, with a few exceptions, from late March through mid-August, the S&P 500 is down nearly 90 points from Oct. 7.

The Nasdaq composite , meanwhile, is down more than 1,100 points over the last two weeks, hitting its lowest point in more than a month on Tuesday.

The S&P 500’s information technology sector, which includes AI-focused firms such as Microsoft and Nvidia, is also down by more than 500 points from two weeks ago.

“If those [tech] stocks don’t do well, it’s pretty hard for the stock market to do much of anything,” Steve Sosnick, chief strategist at Interactive Brokers, told The Hill.

Bond yields in the U.S. and globally have increased throughout the last seven months, as high oil prices amid the Iran war and mounting government deficits have compelled investors to flee the market .

The 10-year U.S. Treasury bond yield is down roughly 25 basis points from Oct. 7, when it reached a 24-year high of 5.365 percent during intraday trading.

But the note remains more than a full percentage point above where it stood at closing time on Feb. 27, the day before the U.S. and Israel launched strikes on Iran .

The 30-year Treasury bond yield has also declined over the last two weeks, falling from 5.733 percent during intraday trading on Oct. 8 to under 5.45 percent this week.

The persistent demand for AI data centers and models, which has spurred a swell in borrowing by major tech firms, is partially contributing to the bond market sell-off, Sosnick argued.

“There’s more demand for money because it’s not only governments demanding money,” he said. “It’s not only the normal amounts of corporations demanding money.”

“It’s that you have this hugely expensive AI build-out that demands money,” Sosnick noted, adding tech companies “used to spin off loads of cash” before the AI boom.

Dan Alpert, the executive chairman at Westwood Capital, said the AI industry is “debt dependent,” as companies are borrowing off their balance sheets to pay for leases for land to construct data centers.

The companies leading the build-out — Amazon, CoreWeave, Google, Meta, Microsoft and Oracle — had issued $193 billion in bonds as of early August, way up from $16.7 billion in 2024, according to data from LSEG.

Investment in data centers, networking infrastructure and other equipment critical to the AI build-out from last year until 2032 will total $10.3 trillion, according to research from the Brookings Institution.

“The notion that that can go on forever is ridiculous,” Alpert told The Hill, later predicting that advancing AI models will “distill each other’s data” and render infrastructure outdated.

“So you have to replace that infrastructure,” Alpert added. “So it’s a big … problem, and I think that the markets are just coming to grips with it.”

Tech analyst Dan Ives acknowledged tech stocks are in a “white-knuckle period,” alluding to investors’ concerns about CoreWeave’s mounting debt.

But Ives, a partner and the senior managing director at Yorkville Ives & Co., predicted earnings reports from tech companies this week will “stabilize” the market.

“I view this as more of a golden opportunity to own the winners rather than the time to panic and listen to the bears that have called 10 of the last two downturns,” he told The Hill.

Stijn Van Nieuwerburgh, a Columbia University professor who authored the Brookings study, wrote the projected AI build-out would occupy a larger segment of the U.S. economy than the canal, railroad, electrification, highway and telecommunications investment booms.

As borrowing costs for that build-out pile up, shares of major tech firms such as Google, Microsoft and Nvidia are down by double digits in recent weeks.

The dip, Sosnick argued, stems from investors “starting to question” whether firms are borrowing “wisely.”

He added, “Maybe not every one of these investments is going to be paying off in a huge, huge way.”

Ives had a more bullish view, arguing that paying back AI-related debt “should not be a problem for the well-positioned players” in the tech industry.

Those firms will make up for companies that cannot pay back their debts, he added.

“Those participating on the credit or debt side will command more money, or more risk, from those players to build it out. And if they can’t pay that, then others will be able to take up that slack,” Ives said, adding he views the AI race as a “Game of Thrones”-style battle between firms.

“There’s banks that fail every year,” he later noted. “The banking system doesn’t fail. You see what I’m saying? So I just view it as … survival of the fittest, and it’s trying to make sure that you differentiate … the winners and the losers.”

Looking ahead, Sosnick argued the stock market’s future performance over the short-term will partially “depend” on Anthropic’s initial public offering (IPO), further proving how critical AI is to the stock market.

Anthropic, which announced over the weekend it will commit 5 percent of its shares to a new public benefit fund, is preparing for an IPO as soon as next month.

“We’re kind of all in on AI, whether we want to be or not,” Sosnick added.

Higher borrowing costs indicated by increased bond yields, therefore, will create a tricky problem for tech firms over the long term. Despite a recent slide, the 10- and 30-year notes are still respectively up by nearly 50 points and 20 points since the start of September.

The fundamentals that spurred the bond market sell-off also remain. Annual inflation was up to 3.7 percent last month, according to the consumer price index, while energy prices remain elevated due to the Iran war and the national debt is above $40.3 trillion.

Persistent inflation spurred Federal Reserve officials to raise interest rates by a quarter point last month, with all 100 economists Reuters recently surveyed expecting the central bank to hike rates again in December.

More than 90 percent of those economists predicted that Fed officials will hold interest rates steady at a range of 3.75 percent to 4 percent at their meeting next week.

Future monetary policy tightening and subsequent “concerns” about borrowing could slow down the AI build-out and “unravel” the market, Sosnick said.

“But I would not say that we’re in a situation yet where people are truly freaking out by any means,” he noted.

articles.title: The anti-AI writing police are everywhere. What are they looking for?
articles.summary: AI writing scandals have exploded over the last year, but there are big questions about who gets accused and why.
articles.body: On October 6, the Zimbabwean author Simbarashe Kundizeza won the Caine Prize for African Writing, for the short story “The Blue Fighter.” Less than a week later, The Atlantic published a piece declaring that the story’s narrator “has all the personality of a chatbot.” “The AI detector Pangram flags almost the entire story as AI-generated,” the article reported. Kundizeza denied that he had used any such technology. “For the avoidance of doubt, I wrote ‘The Blue Fighter.’ I did not use generative AI to write it. It is entirely my own work,” he wrote in a statement on X. The Caine Prize, which comes with a £10,000 award, had become the newest front in a war engulfing the literary world, powered by AI writing tools and AI writing detectors. Scandals about suspected AI use have spread up and down the writing industry this year. In March, the publisher Hachette canceled the US release of author Mia Ballard’s self-published 2025 novel “Shy Girl” after a New York Times report found that it may have been written using AI. In May, a Trinidadian author named Jamir Nazir was accused of using AI to write “The Serpent in the Grove,” which won the Commonwealth Short Story Prize. In July, researchers at Stony Brook University posited that H.M. Wolfe’s “Daggermouth,” a national bestseller, was 60% AI-written according to a data set shared with The Atlantic. More accusations kept flying: debut author Jerry Falade lost a $2 million book deal in July after his agents pulled his debut novel over suspicions he had used AI writing tools. In September, a claim that a book by Haitian Canadian author Thélyson Orélien had failed an AI detection test led the jury for the prestigious Goncourt prize to remove him from its longlist. As generative AI proliferates, it’s easier than ever for an author, or someone who wants to be seen as an author, to come up with a story- or book-shaped piece of text. It’s harder than ever for a reader or a prize judge or a publisher to be sure that the words on a page were produced by human thought and effort, rather than a machine prompt. The result is a literary version of the ruined world in the movie “Blade Runner.” Anxiety and suspicion about robot infiltrators are everywhere — and so are people claiming to hunt the robots down. Multiple companies now offer products that promise to spot the difference, with often contradictory, biased or erratic results. The makers of Pangram, an AI detection platform that has been cited as authoritative in many of the recent controversies, claim it can distinguish between human and synthetic writing with near-perfect accuracy. “We’re trying to mitigate some of the harms that come from these powerful AI models,” said Max Spero, the CEO and founder of Pangram. Spero is quick to admit that he doesn’t have a background in literature or creative writing. He is a machine learning engineer by trade, and worked as a software engineer at Google and an autonomous vehicle startup called Nuro before founding Pangram in 2023. “I’m an avid reader. I’ve never been a writer. I haven’t lived in that world,” Spero said. Nevertheless, Spero presents Pangram as a protector of the magazines and journals that make up the literary ecosystem. “A lot of these outlets are getting flooded with submissions because they pay writers they publish and don’t charge anything to send in your work,” Spero said. “There are these perverse incentives that come from AI making it nearly free. Our goal is to help reduce the friction on the defensive side to help people understand what’s AI and what’s not.” What does a robot sound like? Pangram caught widespread public attention in May, after the Commonwealth Foundation announced that Nazir’s “The Serpent in the Grove” was among the winners of its competition. The story was ornately written, with figurative language that struck some readers as extravagant or peculiar: “Hard living lays itself on a man like wet sacking; it never asks permission. His eyes narrowed against the glare outside and the darker glare inside him: old promises that never ripened, the ache where hope should live, a gnawing sense that land can own a man while making him swear the land belongs to him.” But many people declared they saw telltale tics of chatbot writing. A folklore has quickly grown up around generative AI prose, describing various shibboleths that are supposed to betray the robot voice. One early AI panic revolved around the alleged overuse of em-dashes — an especially funny notion to the many magazine journalists who’d been using them for in-sentence digressions for years — while other people swear the giveaways are “It’s not X, but Y,” grandiose descriptions like “load-bearing,” or lists of three things. The reason such devices show up in AI writing, though, is that they were already in common usage among the legions of human writers whose work AI companies ingested to train their systems. “AI slop is sort of indistinguishable from human-written slop because the AI is trained on bad writing,” said the author Patrick Nathan. “The reason AI writes badly is because the vast majority of writing is bad.” To back up their confidence that something was wrong with the style of the story, then, the people accusing Nazir of using AI also appealed to Pangram numbers. “Pangram flags at 100% but also, come on, if you know you know,” Ethan Mollick, a professor at the Wharton School of the University of Pennsylvania, wrote on Bluesky. Others posted screenshots of the story’s Pangram results like trophies. It’s not lost on the writing community that some of the most gleeful AI hunters, like the tools they use, come from the tech sector, not from among their own ranks. Readers trying to understand what was going on with “The Serpent in the Grove” could encounter Nabeel S. Qureshi, a former engineer at Palantir, posting on X about “the ‘hums’ trope, and plenty of other obvious markers of AI writing.” Suspicious patterns of suspicion There’s also the glaring question of whose work gets fed into Pangram for investigation, and why. The originally anonymous accusation against Orélien was made by Samuel Fitoussi, a conservative French newspaper columnist at Le Figaro and the author of the book “Woke Fiction.” Many of the major scandals were also centered on nonwhite writers; Nazir is of South Asian descent, while Ballard, Wolfe, Falade, Kundizeza and Orélien are Black. “Part of this has to do with a broader anti-woke and anti-Black tenor in a lot of conservative and right-leaning online discourse,” said Doyle D. Calhoun, a professor of postcolonial studies at the University of Cambridge. Calhoun said that for decades the literary establishment was made up mostly of white men. Now that those demographics are changing and there are more non-white authors getting book deals and winning awards, there’s an emerging resentment, especially on social media. “Once these accusations — many of them sort of unverified or unfounded — are out there, the internet media ecosystem just goes into sort of overdrive,” he said. Historically, these sorts of claims also tend not to “stick” to white writers in the same way they do with non-white writers, Calhoun said. Spero said that Pangram is calibrated to call something AI-assisted only if the tool is extremely confident in its analysis. The company’s own estimates claim that false positives — in which the tool wrongly reports that a piece of human writing was created — are 1 in 10,000 and shrinking. Peer-reviewed studies from the University of Chicago and the University of Brussels support that claim, though one 2025 study from the University of Maryland found that Pangram erroneously labeled 2% of documents as AI. A widely referenced 2023 Stanford study that found AI writing detectors produced higher rates of false positives on writing from non-native English speakers was conducted before Pangram was created. Pangram ran an internal study using a database of non-native English texts and self-reported that false positive rate was around 8 in 10,000. How do you prove you’re not a machine? Prior to the emergence of AI writing tools, the cardinal sin of writing was plagiarism. But plagiarism requires two different parties and a measurable accusation. When one author steals another’s words, everyone can judge whether that’s actually the case or not. It’s not that simple with AI writing. Publishing houses are twitchy about putting out potentially AI-written books and authors are tense about being accused of using AI to write lest they be asked to share their drafts and version history with the entire internet. Social networks are so inundated with AI writing —both real and imagined — that LinkedIn has installed a new post reaction option: “Looks like AI slop.” Given the thousands upon thousands of pieces of writing published each day, a 1 in 10,000 chance of a false accusation — let alone an 8 in 10,000 chance — means that even the most trusted AI detector is going to be wrong, and wrong about a lot of people. Pangram isn’t able to tell users the truth about someone’s writing, but it is able to introduce something much more complicated: doubt. Unless an accused writer confesses to using an LLM, there is no bulletproof way to prove an accusation, short of being given full access to someone’s computer history and finding the chatbot prompts. The Caine Prize judges said that they would using a “human centered approach” to determine the provenance of Kundieza’s story. Ellah Wakatama, chair of the Caine Prize’s board of trustees, told the BBC that the writer would send his draft history to the organization for review. While draft version histories are not sacred texts, being asked to share them in exchange for exoneration does introduce some thorny social questions about how much writers need to show an audience — or accuser — in order to be trusted. And once an accusation is made, there’s no consensus about what evidence would be sufficient to clear an author’s name. When Bryan Armen Graham, a sports editor at The Guardian, was accused of using AI to help him write articles, the publication called the allegations “preposterous.” That didn’t stop several others, including some journalists, from siding with the Pangram results over the word of a colleague. Either way, a machine wins To some people and institutions on the literary side, using automated AI writing detectors to fight the influx of AI writing is just trading one form of technological domination for another. Pangram has entered the public consciousness at a time of distrust that goes beyond writing. “All of this is happening in a larger milieu of bullshit,” said John Warner, the author of “More Than Words: How to Think About Writing in the Age of AI.” The ability to dam at least some of the daily overflow of misinformation and misrepresentation is one of the reasons for Pangram’s success and adoption, but Warner said that comes at a cost. “Like all other technology of automation, that is going to de-skill people from discerning these things for themselves,” he said. The Commonwealth Foundation conducted a review of the work of Nazir and the other nominees, but it chose not to use Pangram or other AI detection software in the process. “Because the tools aren’t conclusive the jury is still out as to how much they can be relied upon,” Razmi Farook, director general of the Commonwealth Foundation, said. “For us, we didn’t want to rely on a singular indicator. We believe the fairest approach is to consider multiple sources of evidence.” Those sources, Farook said, included the original reading and judging process, along with “supporting documentation” of the writers’ “creative processes, including working drafts, notes, and other relevant materials.” There were also lengthy discussions with each author about how their stories came together. Snippets of those conversations were included in a video promoting the award. The foundation concluded that none of the writers, including Nazir, had used AI tools to write their stories. But the literary magazine Granta, which had published the story as part of an agreement with the Commonwealth Foundation, canceled its relationship for future competitions. Sigrid Rausing, Granta’s publisher, said in a statement that the magazine fed Nazir’s story into Claude as a way of gauging whether it was written with AI. “The response was long, concluding that it was ‘almost certainly not produced unaided by a human,’” wrote Rausing. (Claude is not designed to detect AI writing.) The statement from Granta was far from conclusive, though, and it summed up the anxious ambivalence that many authors and readers are feeling in the AI age. “It may be that the judges have now awarded a prize to an instance of AI plagiarism — we don’t yet know, and perhaps we never will know,” Rausing wrote. “There is, however, a certain irony in the fact that beyond human hunches AI itself is the most efficient tool we have for revealing what is AI generated.” Spero was unconvinced by the foundation’s investigation, but offered to take down a case study posted to the Pangram website if they shared the results and he was satisfied with the process. The foundation refused, citing legal and privacy issues. Farook said, however, that her team has asked Pangram for their input on how to secure the award process next year.

articles.title: One week after crushing neocloud stocks like CoreWeave and Nebius with a single word, SpaceX's Elon Musk is out with another word that is less dire
articles.summary: It should never cease to amaze the power of the world’s richest person Elon Musk to move a stock or sector with a single word.
articles.body:
It should never cease to amaze the power of the world's richest person Elon Musk to move a stock or sector with a single word.

Recall, a week ago the rise in yields on CoreWeave's ( CRWV ) bonds spurred Musk to post "Yikes" on X in response to a post by venture capitalist Chamath Palihapitiya. You never want to see Musk say "yikes" on anything related to CoreWeave — or anything more broadly.

The word helped fuel a rout in shares of CoreWeave and other neocloud stocks such as Nebius ( NBIS ).

Musk was back on SpaceX's ( SPCX ) earnings call late Tuesday with a different word, a bone thrown to the neocloud bulls if you will: "ridiculous." That is, talk of excess capacity on the AI infrastructure front is ridiculous given the demand being seen for the tech.

"It is ridiculous. I do not think we are going to have a demand issue here. I am not saying this will happen, it is not impossible that we will have a six-month payback period for compute next year," Musk said.

Shares of CoreWeave gained 2% in pre-market trading on Wednesday amid Musk's more upbeat tone, with Nebius up 2%. IREN Limited ( IREN ) advanced 3%.

SpaceX delivered a solid third-quarter earnings report.

Revenue of $14.58 billion grew 161% from the prior year and beat analyst estimates of $12.7 billion. EPS of $0.35 clocked in $0.20 ahead of analyst forecasts.

The company's Space, Connectivity and Superintelligence businesses all grew revenue year over year.

"I walked away feeling there is momentum at least through 2027 in terms of demand and that feels longer than the market's current perception. This my be one step forward in a series of important upcoming AI-related catalysts," 22V Research analyst Dauvin Peterson said. "Neoclouds will earn a position in this debate on both sides of the house. First, the bullish market pricing commentary and the tighter-for-longer commentary should bode well for neoclouds that are similarly building on Nvidia compute into 2027 and beyond and which can demonstrate the capability to also access a strong pricing environment."

Brian Sozzi is Yahoo Finance's Executive Editor, host of the Sozzi Unleashed morning show and the Power Players with Brian Sozzi podcast, and a member of Yahoo Finance's editorial leadership team.

articles.title: The feds are opening a front door for crypto markets
articles.summary: The lack of a new law is no excuse for a lack of clear rules under the laws we already have.
articles.body:
On Oct. 5 , the Commodity Futures Trading Commission opened a federal front door for America’s crypto exchanges. Its advance notice on Regulation Crypto Asset Transactions and Regulation Crypto Asset Markets sets out how exchanges that let everyday customers trade crypto on margin, with leverage or financing, could register and operate under one national set of rules.

That matters. Today most U.S. crypto exchanges are licensed state-by-state as money transmitters , in the same category as check cashers and gift-card sellers. Those licenses police fraud and money laundering. They were never designed to police markets and oversee orderly trading, manipulation, conflicts of interest and the safekeeping of customer assets. The CFTC’s plan would fill that gap for the firms that choose it.

Some will ask whether the agency is overreaching, given that Congress failed to pass the Clarity Act . It is not. The CFTC is not claiming any new power. It is finally writing rules for a power Congress gave it in 2010.

Under the Commodity Exchange Act , added by Dodd-Frank, retail commodity trades offered on a leveraged, margined or financed basis are treated as if they were futures. They must take place on a CFTC-registered exchange unless the commodity is actually delivered within 28 days . Federal courts have held that bitcoin and other virtual currencies are commodities under the act.

The CFTC has enforced that provision against crypto firms for years . But what it never did was explain how a firm could comply. The new framework uses the same statute, the same exchange core principles it contains , and the same customer protections that already govern futures brokers. It also leaves spot-only exchanges where Congress left them: under state law, unless they opt in. Now that courts have more leeway to read statutes for themselves rather than deferring to agencies , that close fit to the text is a strength.

The policy case is just as strong. First, it protects ordinary investors. Exchanges would have to show that the tokens they list are not easily manipulated , weighing who holds the supply, when insiders’ tokens unlock, and whether new tokens are minted or bought back.

Customer money would be handled by regulated brokers, subject to capital, segregation, disclosure and anti-money-laundering rules. Exchanges that hold customers’ crypto in one pooled account could be required to show they have enough on hand to pay everyone back.

Second, this CFTC action brings the business home. As I recount in my new book, years of regulation-by-enforcement pushed builders and capital offshore. A clear, workable path to registration invites them back under American rules and American oversight.

Third, it respects choice. As in our dual banking system, a firm can pick a state license or a federal registration based on what it offers. And by confirming that delivery to a customer’s own wallet within 28 days counts as “actual delivery,” the CFTC leaves room for self-custody and onchain finance.

None of this replaces legislation. Only Congress can require every crypto exchange to register federally, and it should still act to do so. But the lack of a new law is no excuse for a lack of clear rules under the laws we already have.

In 2018, I told the Senate that we owed a new generation of crypto enthusiasts a thoughtful and balanced response, not a dismissive one . Monday’s proposal is that response. It is an early step, and the details will matter. Exchanges, investors and builders should use the comment period to help the CFTC get them right.

Mr. Giancarlo served as the 13 th chairman of the U.S. Commodity Futures Trading Commission. He is the author of the forthcoming book “The New Adventures of CryptoDad: the Quest for Financial Freedom in the 21st Century.” Current CFTC Chairman Michael Selig, who once clerked for Giancarlo, is a former colleague of his in private law practice.

articles.title: Netflix has 2 problems behind the stock slide — and they aren't YouTube, co-CEO Ted Sarandos says
articles.summary: Netflix has several key challenges that won't be fixed overnight.
articles.body:
Netflix ( NFLX ) is seeing its viewership come under increasing siege from the behemoth that is Alphabet's ( GOOG , GOOGL ) YouTube, but the two main issues it will have to confront as it seeks to arrest a major stock slide this year are more internal.

And they can't be fixed immediately by laying off 6% of the workforce and, surprisingly, by pushing out Bela Bajaria as chief content officer in favor of former Disney ( DIS ) exec Peter Rice, as seen this week.

In the end, a Netflix growth reboot will hinge on a steady pipeline of fresh creative talent and more content home runs.

"Most importantly, Rob, Peter Rice understands talent relations, and in a competitive market, creative talent have choices of where they want to work, and we want Netflix to always be the place that they love to do the best work of their life. Peter is the exact right person to lead those efforts in the U.S. and around the world," Netflix co-CEO Ted Sarandos said on the company's earnings call late Tuesday.

"The U.S. is also working," he continued. "It's just not growing as fast as it could or as fast as we'd like. We had some really solid doubles and triples this year. But the other territories count on some of those titles being home runs so that they'll travel around the world."

Netflix delivered a mixed third quarter earnings report amid those doubles and triples on the content front, with earnings of $0.87 per share, beating Wall Street estimates of $0.82.

Revenue of $12.87 billion came in line with analysts' expectations.

For the fourth quarter, Netflix forecast revenue of $13.44 billion, below expectations of $13.57 billion.

The company also cut its full-year advertising revenue outlook to about $2.7 billion from $3 billion previously.

Netflix stock fell 6% in premarket trading. The stock had been down 26% this year ahead of the earnings release.
